questions.q: What is a database transaction, as described in this lesson?
options: A single SELECT statement
A set of writes that become permanent together, or not at all
A backup of the entire database
A connection string
questions.explain: A transaction's defining guarantee is all-or-nothing: either every write in it commits, or none do.

options: Permanently deletes the target table
Discards every uncommitted change in the current transaction
Reconnects to the database automatically
Commits all pending changes immediately
questions.explain: rollback() undoes uncommitted writes, returning the database to its state before the transaction began.

questions.q: Why catch pyodbc.Error before a bare except Exception?
options: Because pyodbc.Error is slower to catch
Order doesn't matter in Python
To handle the specific, expected database errors first, then catch and re-raise anything unexpected
Because except Exception is not valid Python syntax
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 16's pattern: handle what you expect specifically, then don't silently swallow the rest.

questions.q: In the load_rows() function shown in this lesson, when does the rollback happen?
options: Before the INSERT statements run
Only if the function is called twice
If a pyodbc.Error is raised during the TRUNCATE or INSERT statements
Every single time the function runs, regardless of success
questions.explain: The rollback only fires inside the except block, when a pyodbc.Error actually occurs.

questions.q: Why does the TRUNCATE in the rollback example also get undone if the INSERT fails afterward?
options: TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back under any circumstances
Both statements are part of the same uncommitted transaction, so rollback() discards all of it
TRUNCATE runs in a completely separate connection
It doesn't get undone - only the INSERT does
questions.explain: Since commit() was never reached, both the TRUNCATE and the INSERT attempt belong to one transaction.
